doc.title: David Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2022

title: Can you go beyond Ascension; Banff workshop and approach
summary: Weiss says nobody sets out to innovate, recalls Banff under Dave Holland with Muhal Richard Abrams, and says the Cookers' approach matters most, as Billy Hart's comment on records shows.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: When you look at the arts, music and the visual arts especially, sometimes I wonder if it gets harder to innovate? What do you do that’s beyond Coltrane’s “Ascension” or any number of examples of how the limits of the art was pushed? How do you go beyond that and still create something that people might accept?
Well when you put it that way it sounds like a problem.
Well you can put it in a different way. I’d be happy if you did.

No, I’m half kidding, but half kind of acknowledging. I think what happens is I don’t think anybody really tried to be an innovator. I think a lot of it was just natural growth. And the interesting thing is a friend I work with came back from Banff. I went to Banff right out of college. It’s a jazz workshop in the Canadian Rockies. When I went there Dave Holland was running the program. So coming out of North Texas State kind of, I needed to listen up a little bit let’s say, and that’s actually where Muhal Richard Abrams was the guest conductor and we did a concert with him playing his music. But Dave Holland ran it. Dave Liebman and Richie Beirach were there, George Lewis, I don’t know if you know him he was an avante garde trombone player. He was there. John Abercrombie was there. I’m trying to think of who else — Kenny Wheeler was there. Guys that were pretty much rooted in stuff but also trying to be — you know. I think it’s just an approach and what happens happens. I think nobody can sit there and go like, “Well it’s time to change music today.” But it’s definitely an approach. Again, you know, I go back to the Cookers ‘cause there’s just not many examples. Those guys are, I mean I’ll recognize things they played from another time and I’m definitely guilty of it, but they’re always pushing something. They’re always trying something. It’s just an approach, and the approach is the most important thing. You know? Never staying pat, just you know always pushing things. Everything seems fresh with them. You know there’s no — I mean there might be a routine within it, I mean on this material we’ve definitely, I mean to put it in, it’s not the right way to put it, it’s actually the most wrong way I could put it, they’ve developed routines. I mean that’s not the word I want to use when I’m talking about openness and freedom and stuff. But they’ve developed stuff within the tune but really what they’re doing is using it as a launching pad to go somewhere. So I mean it was an interesting conversation I had with Billy Hart. We had done two records, Billy more than once was telling me like, “You know what? There are two very good records. I like these. I don’t say that often but I like these two.” And I called him up and said, “Hey we got offered to do a third record.” And he said, “Why?” And I says like, “Well because we do this for a living? We keep making records.” And what he meant was we found the material that we need to do what we do. Why do more? I said well you never know. We might find a couple more. And we definitely have, but the conversation went to okay why did Miles Davis and Wayne Shorter and Herbie, Ron
